newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to raise 1998 military spending for reform.
newsitem.headline: Russia to raise 1998 military spending for reform.

text.p: Russia will boost defence spending next year to 94 trillion roubles ($16.3 billion) from 83 trillion in 1997 to carry out long-delayed military reforms, Interfax news agency quoted a senior minister as saying.

Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Yakov Urinson told Interfax late on Thursday defence spending was one of the key issues of next year's budget, and that expenditure would be increased annually.
In 1996, Russia spent 64 trillion on national defence.
"The 94 trillion budgeted for 1998 is a considerable increase which will allow us to find the means to carry out military reform," Urinson said. Interfax published his comments on Friday.

The structure of military spending would be changed, focusing on purchases of modern military equipment, research and combat training -- in line with recent statements from new Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev.
The same priorities would apply in financing law enforcement and state security bodies, Urinson added. Russia plans to spend 47 trillion roubles on these next year.

Sergeyev declared war on waste in the army earlier this week by committing himself to a long campaign that will trim and modernise Moscow's vast but obsolescent armed forces, junking outdated hardware to invest in state-of-the-art equipment.

But the concept of increasing military expenditure, which Urinson said was approved by reformist First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, is hardly in line with President Boris Yeltsin's pledge to cut defence spending to 3.5 percent of gross domestic product by 2000 from five percent now.

Yeltsin sacked his predecessor last month for failing to make progress on the president's goal of a professional, non-conscript force by the turn of the century and for "whining" too often about the army's need for more money.
Chubais heads a committee in charge of financing the modernisation of the demoralised Cold War-era army.
The head of the air force said on Wednesday its personnel would be cut by more than a third by 2001, in line with similar reductions across the board.

Russia's armed forces are estimated to be about 1.8 million men strong but even generals concede they are not sure of the exact figure, making it hard to assess progress on previous plans to cut 200,000 men this year. ($1=5,761 roubles)
